tools.name: vm_troubleshoot
tools.description: Diagnose KubeVirt VirtualMachine issues with automated root-cause detection. Collects VM status, VMI status, volumes, DataVolume/PVC state, cloud-init configuration, pod state, logs, and events, then runs heuristic checks to identify specific problems and suggest fixes. Returns a 'Detected Issues' section with CRITICAL/WARNING findings and actionable remediation steps, followed by raw diagnostic data. Use this tool FIRST whenever a user asks why a VM is not starting, stuck in Provisioning, crashlooping, failing to migrate, or exhibiting unexpected behavior. Automatically detects: missing StorageClasses, invalid PVC specs, dangerous cloud-init commands (shutdown/halt), nodeSelector migration blockers, failed migrations, and pod crashloops. If the user asks to fix or remediate the issue, use the Suggested Fixes from the report with vm_lifecycle (restart) or resources_create_or_update.

name.description: The name of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

namespace.description: The namespace of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - replicas: 2
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - container name: rec-engine
  - containerPort: 80 (matching stable)
  - security configuration: same as stable (no additional securityContext)
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - selector changed to app: recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1
  - left port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), matching the existing stable setup

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1 behind the same Service, Kubernetes will distribute traffic roughly 50/50 between stable and canary.

Quick verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | grep -A3 selector
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

Rollback (if needed)
- Point Service back to stable only:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns patch svc recommendation-engine --type merge -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"recommendation-engine","version":"v2.0"}}}'
- Remove the canary:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns delete deploy engine-v2-1

Notes
- Traffic weighting is approximate and based on the number of ready endpoints. Keeping 2 pods on each deployment yields ~50/50. Adjust replica counts or use a service mesh/ingress with weighted routing for precise control.

deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - replicas: 2
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - container name: rec-engine
  - containerPort: 80 (matching stable)
  - security configuration: same as stable (no additional securityContext)
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - selector changed to app: recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1
  - left port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), matching the existing stable setup

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1 behind the same Service, Kubernetes will distribute traffic roughly 50/50 between stable and canary.

Quick verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | grep -A3 selector
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

Rollback (if needed)
- Point Service back to stable only:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns patch svc recommendation-engine --type merge -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"recommendation-engine","version":"v2.0"}}}'
- Remove the canary:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns delete deploy engine-v2-1

Notes
- Traffic weighting is approximate and based on the number of ready endpoints. Keeping 2 pods on each deployment yields ~50/50. Adjust replica counts or use a service mesh/ingress with weighted routing for precise control.

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - replicas: 2
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - container name: rec-engine
  - containerPort: 80 (matching stable)
  - security configuration: same as stable (no additional securityContext)
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - selector changed to app: recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1
  - left port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), matching the existing stable setup

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1 behind the same Service, Kubernetes will distribute traffic roughly 50/50 between stable and canary.

Quick verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | grep -A3 selector
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

Rollback (if needed)
- Point Service back to stable only:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns patch svc recommendation-engine --type merge -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"recommendation-engine","version":"v2.0"}}}'
- Remove the canary:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns delete deploy engine-v2-1

Notes
- Traffic weighting is approximate and based on the number of ready endpoints. Keeping 2 pods on each deployment yields ~50/50. Adjust replica counts or use a service mesh/ingress with weighted routing for precise control.

- Kept the container image as quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and exposed containerPort 8080.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but:
  - The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing probe failures and the app to be marked unavailable.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic to the Service couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (port stays 80 for clients).
- Result: rollout completed and the app is healthy.
  - Deployment webapp: 1/1 available
  - Pod webapp-…: 1/1 Ready
  - Service webapp: ClusterIP 10.96.119.63, port 80 -> targetPort 8080

How you can verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy,pod,svc
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.4.0 -- sh -lc 'curl -sS http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/'

Do you need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can set up an Ingress (or LoadBalancer/NodePort) if you want it reachable from outside the cluster. Tell me the desired hostname/path (e.g., orders.example.com) and I’ll configure it.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I investigated and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but:
  - The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing probe failures and the app to be marked unavailable.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic to the Service couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (port stays 80 for clients).
- Result: rollout completed and the app is healthy.
  - Deployment webapp: 1/1 available
  - Pod webapp-…: 1/1 Ready
  - Service webapp: ClusterIP 10.96.119.63, port 80 -> targetPort 8080

How you can verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy,pod,svc
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.4.0 -- sh -lc 'curl -sS http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/'

Do you need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can set up an Ingress (or LoadBalancer/NodePort) if you want it reachable from outside the cluster. Tell me the desired hostname/path (e.g., orders.example.com) and I’ll configure it.

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but:
  - The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing probe failures and the app to be marked unavailable.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic to the Service couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Probes now GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (port stays 80 for clients).
- Result: rollout completed and the app is healthy.
  - Deployment webapp: 1/1 available
  - Pod webapp-…: 1/1 Ready
  - Service webapp: ClusterIP 10.96.119.63, port 80 -> targetPort 8080

How you can verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy,pod,svc
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.4.0 -- sh -lc 'curl -sS http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/'

Do you need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can set up an Ingress (or LoadBalancer/NodePort) if you want it reachable from outside the cluster. Tell me the desired hostname/path (e.g., orders.example.com) and I’ll configure it.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account did not grant any permissions on Pods. It only allowed listing Deployments (apiGroup: apps), so listing pods failed.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include core Pods permissions and kept the existing Deployments rule:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
    - resources: pods
    - verbs: get, list, watch
  - apiGroup: apps
    - resources: deployments
    - verbs: list

Your existing RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already targets the pod-reader ServiceAccount, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- If you have permission to impersonate:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods
  - Should return “yes”.
- Or run a Pod that uses serviceAccountName: pod-reader and use any client to call the API to list pods in the namespace.

You should now be able to list pods with the pod-reader service account in simple-rbac-setup.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account did not grant any permissions on Pods. It only allowed listing Deployments (apiGroup: apps), so listing pods failed.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include core Pods permissions and kept the existing Deployments rule:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
    - resources: pods
    - verbs: get, list, watch
  - apiGroup: apps
    - resources: deployments
    - verbs: list

Your existing RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already targets the pod-reader ServiceAccount, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- If you have permission to impersonate:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods
  - Should return “yes”.
- Or run a Pod that uses serviceAccountName: pod-reader and use any client to call the API to list pods in the namespace.

You should now be able to list pods with the pod-reader service account in simple-rbac-setup.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service was selecting the wrong pods: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80, so even with the right selector, traffic would have hit the wrong port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service in web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080 (port remains 80)
- Result: Endpoints now show 10.244.0.50:8080 for Service nginx, and an EndpointSlice exists with port 8080. The Deployment is Ready.

Current state (summary)
- Service: web/nginx ClusterIP 10.96.128.163 port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.50:8080 present
- Pods: nginx-… Running and Ready

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- Run a quick test pod and curl the service:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.7.1 -- sh -lc 'curl -sSI http://nginx | head -n1'
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- Option A: NodePort (example picks 30080)
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort","ports":[{"port":80,"targetPort":8080,"nodePort":30080}]}}'
  - Then reach http://<node-ip>:30080
- Option B: Ingress (preferred with an Ingress controller)
  - I can create an Ingress for a hostname you provide (e.g., nginx.example.com) pointing to Service nginx:80.

Would you like me to expose it externally (NodePort or Ingress)?

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service was selecting the wrong pods: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80, so even with the right selector, traffic would have hit the wrong port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service in web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080 (port remains 80)
- Result: Endpoints now show 10.244.0.50:8080 for Service nginx, and an EndpointSlice exists with port 8080. The Deployment is Ready.

Current state (summary)
- Service: web/nginx ClusterIP 10.96.128.163 port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.50:8080 present
- Pods: nginx-… Running and Ready

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- Run a quick test pod and curl the service:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.7.1 -- sh -lc 'curl -sSI http://nginx | head -n1'
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- Option A: NodePort (example picks 30080)
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort","ports":[{"port":80,"targetPort":8080,"nodePort":30080}]}}'
  - Then reach http://<node-ip>:30080
- Option B: Ingress (preferred with an Ingress controller)
  - I can create an Ingress for a hostname you provide (e.g., nginx.example.com) pointing to Service nginx:80.

Would you like me to expose it externally (NodePort or Ingress)?

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service was selecting the wrong pods: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80, so even with the right selector, traffic would have hit the wrong port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service in web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080 (port remains 80)
- Result: Endpoints now show 10.244.0.50:8080 for Service nginx, and an EndpointSlice exists with port 8080. The Deployment is Ready.

Current state (summary)
- Service: web/nginx ClusterIP 10.96.128.163 port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.50:8080 present
- Pods: nginx-… Running and Ready

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- Run a quick test pod and curl the service:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.7.1 -- sh -lc 'curl -sSI http://nginx | head -n1'
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- Option A: NodePort (example picks 30080)
  - kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort","ports":[{"port":80,"targetPort":8080,"nodePort":30080}]}}'
  - Then reach http://<node-ip>:30080
- Option B: Ingress (preferred with an Ingress controller)
  - I can create an Ingress for a hostname you provide (e.g., nginx.example.com) pointing to Service nginx:80.

Would you like me to expose it externally (NodePort or Ingress)?

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Root causes
- Pods weren’t scheduling: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label. Events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector. Result: 0 endpoints behind the Service.
- Port mismatch: The nginx container listens on 8080 (default.conf: listen 8080), but the Service was targeting port 80. Even with pods up, that would cause connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Aligned ports:
  - Updated Service web-app-service to targetPort: 8080 (still exposed as port 80 in-cluster).
  - Set containerPort 8080 in the Deployment and added basic readiness/liveness probes on 8080.

Current status
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Available and Ready.
- Service web-app-service Endpoints now include two pod IPs.
- Nginx is running and listening on 8080 in the pods.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should return the nginx page.
- Check pods: kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
- Check endpoints: kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service -o wide

Notes/next steps
- If you actually need to pin these pods to GPU nodes, re-add the nodeSelector and label the target node(s) with environment=production-gpu (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or switch to node affinity/tolerations as appropriate.
- To avoid port drift issues in the future, consider using a named container port (e.g., name: http, containerPort: 8080) and set Service targetPort: http.

Want me to reintroduce the nodeSelector and label the appropriate node(s), or leave it as-is for now?

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Root causes
- Pods weren’t scheduling: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label. Events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector. Result: 0 endpoints behind the Service.
- Port mismatch: The nginx container listens on 8080 (default.conf: listen 8080), but the Service was targeting port 80. Even with pods up, that would cause connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Aligned ports:
  - Updated Service web-app-service to targetPort: 8080 (still exposed as port 80 in-cluster).
  - Set containerPort 8080 in the Deployment and added basic readiness/liveness probes on 8080.

Current status
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Available and Ready.
- Service web-app-service Endpoints now include two pod IPs.
- Nginx is running and listening on 8080 in the pods.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should return the nginx page.
- Check pods: kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
- Check endpoints: kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service -o wide

Notes/next steps
- If you actually need to pin these pods to GPU nodes, re-add the nodeSelector and label the target node(s) with environment=production-gpu (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or switch to node affinity/tolerations as appropriate.
- To avoid port drift issues in the future, consider using a named container port (e.g., name: http, containerPort: 8080) and set Service targetPort: http.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Root causes
- Pods weren’t scheduling: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label. Events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector. Result: 0 endpoints behind the Service.
- Port mismatch: The nginx container listens on 8080 (default.conf: listen 8080), but the Service was targeting port 80. Even with pods up, that would cause connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Aligned ports:
  - Updated Service web-app-service to targetPort: 8080 (still exposed as port 80 in-cluster).
  - Set containerPort 8080 in the Deployment and added basic readiness/liveness probes on 8080.

Current status
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Available and Ready.
- Service web-app-service Endpoints now include two pod IPs.
- Nginx is running and listening on 8080 in the pods.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should return the nginx page.
- Check pods: kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
- Check endpoints: kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service -o wide

Notes/next steps
- If you actually need to pin these pods to GPU nodes, re-add the nodeSelector and label the target node(s) with environment=production-gpu (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or switch to node affinity/tolerations as appropriate.
- To avoid port drift issues in the future, consider using a named container port (e.g., name: http, containerPort: 8080) and set Service targetPort: http.

- Developers get full access to their own namespaces and read-only access to dev-shared (both as users and via their service accounts).

- Default-deny policies are applied to all created namespaces. DNS egress to kube-system:53 is explicitly allowed. If you need to allow other “system services,” add similar egress rules to the relevant namespaces.

What I created
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (selector app=db)
- StatefulSet: db with 3 replicas
  - Container: busybox:1.36 (sleep loop)
  - initContainer writes initial_data to /data/test if missing
  - volumeClaimTemplates: data, 1Gi, ReadWriteOnce, mounted at /data
  - PVC retention policy: Retain (PVCs persist when scaling down)

Then I scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica.

To enable filesystem reporting, the guest OS must have the QEMU Guest Agent installed and running.

- Linux (Fedora/RHEL/CentOS):
  - sudo dnf install -y qemu-guest-agent
  - sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
- Linux (Ubuntu/Debian):
  - sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y qemu-guest-agent
  - sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
- Windows:

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and fixed for VirtualMachine vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm:

Root cause
- The VM’s virt-launcher pod failed to initialize due to a missing cloud-init Secret.
- Evidence from vm-troubleshoot events: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
- The VM spec references cloudInitNoCloud with secretRef.name=vm-cloud-init, but that Secret did not exist.

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with a basic cloud-init userdata payload.
- Restarted the VM to ensure the virt-launcher pod re-mounts the newly created Secret and proceeds with initialization.

Outcome (verification)
- The VM reports Ready=True and printableStatus=Running after the restart.
- This confirms the mount issue is resolved and the VM is now operational.

Notes and next steps
- I added a simple cloud-init payload. If you require specific user data (users/SSH keys/packages), update the Secret vm-cloud-init (key: userdata) with your desired cloud-config content and restart the VM again if needed.

Steps.message: VM created with missing Secret reference - waiting for failure state

Here’s what I found and fixed for VirtualMachine vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm:

Root cause
- The VM’s virt-launcher pod failed to initialize due to a missing cloud-init Secret.
- Evidence from vm-troubleshoot events: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
- The VM spec references cloudInitNoCloud with secretRef.name=vm-cloud-init, but that Secret did not exist.

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with a basic cloud-init userdata payload.
- Restarted the VM to ensure the virt-launcher pod re-mounts the newly created Secret and proceeds with initialization.

Outcome (verification)
- The VM reports Ready=True and printableStatus=Running after the restart.
- This confirms the mount issue is resolved and the VM is now operational.

Notes and next steps
- I added a simple cloud-init payload. If you require specific user data (users/SSH keys/packages), update the Secret vm-cloud-init (key: userdata) with your desired cloud-config content and restart the VM again if needed.

Root cause
- The VM’s virt-launcher pod failed to initialize due to a missing cloud-init Secret.
- Evidence from vm-troubleshoot events: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
- The VM spec references cloudInitNoCloud with secretRef.name=vm-cloud-init, but that Secret did not exist.

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with a basic cloud-init userdata payload.
- Restarted the VM to ensure the virt-launcher pod re-mounts the newly created Secret and proceeds with initialization.

Outcome (verification)
- The VM reports Ready=True and printableStatus=Running after the restart.
- This confirms the mount issue is resolved and the VM is now operational.

Notes and next steps
- I added a simple cloud-init payload. If you require specific user data (users/SSH keys/packages), update the Secret vm-cloud-init (key: userdata) with your desired cloud-config content and restart the VM again if needed.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

- Root cause
  - The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always and its cloud-init userData instructs the guest to power off immediately after boot. KubeVirt sees the VM shut down and restarts it, creating an endless crash/restart loop.

- Problematic cloud-init command
  - In cloud-init runcmd:
    - shutdown -h now

- How to fix it
  - If you want the VM to stay up: remove the shutdown line from cloud-init userData and re-apply the VM spec, then restart the VM.
  - If the shutdown is intentional after provisioning: change the VM’s runStrategy so it won’t auto-restart on a clean shutdown. Options:
    - runStrategy: Halted (VM remains stopped), or
    - runStrategy: Manual (VM won’t auto-restart), or
    - runStrategy: RerunOnFailure (won’t restart on a clean shutdown, only on failures)

If you want, I can apply either fix for you:
- Remove the shutdown from cloud-init and restart the VM, or
- Update runStrategy to Halted/Manual/RerunOnFailure.

Steps.message: Waiting for VM to attempt boot and crash...

Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

- Root cause
  - The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always and its cloud-init userData instructs the guest to power off immediately after boot. KubeVirt sees the VM shut down and restarts it, creating an endless crash/restart loop.

- Problematic cloud-init command
  - In cloud-init runcmd:
    - shutdown -h now

- How to fix it
  - If you want the VM to stay up: remove the shutdown line from cloud-init userData and re-apply the VM spec, then restart the VM.
  - If the shutdown is intentional after provisioning: change the VM’s runStrategy so it won’t auto-restart on a clean shutdown. Options:
    - runStrategy: Halted (VM remains stopped), or
    - runStrategy: Manual (VM won’t auto-restart), or
    - runStrategy: RerunOnFailure (won’t restart on a clean shutdown, only on failures)

If you want, I can apply either fix for you:
- Remove the shutdown from cloud-init and restart the VM, or
- Update runStrategy to Halted/Manual/RerunOnFailure.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

- Root cause
  - The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always and its cloud-init userData instructs the guest to power off immediately after boot. KubeVirt sees the VM shut down and restarts it, creating an endless crash/restart loop.

- Problematic cloud-init command
  - In cloud-init runcmd:
    - shutdown -h now

- How to fix it
  - If you want the VM to stay up: remove the shutdown line from cloud-init userData and re-apply the VM spec, then restart the VM.
  - If the shutdown is intentional after provisioning: change the VM’s runStrategy so it won’t auto-restart on a clean shutdown. Options:
    - runStrategy: Halted (VM remains stopped), or
    - runStrategy: Manual (VM won’t auto-restart), or
    - runStrategy: RerunOnFailure (won’t restart on a clean shutdown, only on failures)

If you want, I can apply either fix for you:
- Remove the shutdown from cloud-init and restart the VM, or
- Update runStrategy to Halted/Manual/RerunOnFailure.

I tried to retrieve guest info via the QEMU guest agent, but the VM does not have the agent connected yet.

Error:
- VMI test-vm-with-agent does not have guest agent connected (guestOSInfo, filesystems, users, networkInterfaces queries all failed)

This typically means cloud-init is still running or the qemu-guest-agent service hasn’t started in the guest yet.

What the guest agent data will include once available:
- Operating system
  - OS name/distribution, version, variant
  - Kernel release and version
  - Architecture
  - Machine/host ID and pretty name
- Filesystems
  - Device (e.g., /dev/vda1), mount point (/, /boot, /home)
  - Filesystem type (ext4, xfs, btrfs, etc.)
  - Capacity metrics (total, used, available bytes), inode usage
  - Mount options
- Network interfaces
  - Interface name (e.g., eth0, ens3), MAC address
  - IPv4/IPv6 addresses with prefixes
  - Link state, MTU
  - Default gateway and routes
  - DNS servers and search domains
